newsitem.title: CANADA: Winnipeg confidence grows as flood crest falls.
newsitem.headline: Winnipeg confidence grows as flood crest falls.

text.p: Winnipeg's confidence grew on Tuesday as the flooding Red River's crest began to recede, but emergency officials cautioned against succumbing to a false sense of security.
"We're still in the mode of being very vigilant," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said. "We're still on pins and needles for the next two weeks at least."
Dikes in Canada's flood-ravaged Red River Valley took a beating from high winds on Monday but withstood the challenge without any major breaches.

Winds were forecast to gust up to 25 mph (40 kmh) on Tuesday, further battering the flood defenses that have so far saved Winnipeg, Manitoba's biggest city with 650,000 people, from serious damage. Twenty-nine city homes were flooded so far.
"Now that I've got a registration card and food vouchers, I'm really starting to feel like a refugee," south Winnipeg evacuee Marguerite Fouillard said.
Winds should continue on Wednesday with only minimal showers, meteorologist Rick Walls said.
Monday's winds created white caps of up to two feet (60 cm) high on the so-called "Red Sea," an expanse of floodwater twice the size of Hong Kong, which has submerged southern Manitoba.
More than 28,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans have been forced from their homes by the worst flooding since 1852.

"They haven't really said when we can get home but hopefully in the next two weeks," Brigitte Doerkson said. She and her four daughters have been in a Winnipeg evacuation shelter for the past two weeks.
The floods devastated southern Manitoba and North Dakota, causing more than $1 billion in damage.
"The Salvation Army in Winnipeg has collected C$780,000 ($560,000) toward the flood relief effort," Salvation Army spokeswoman Anne Bennett said.
The Mennonite Disaster Service opened offices in Winnipeg and Fargo, N.D., to pump out homes and clean them up, Syd Reimer said.
The Red River level in downtown Winnipeg fell to about 24.2 feet (7.4 meters) early on Tuesday after cresting last Thursday at 24.5 feet (7.5 metres) above winter ice level, a spokesman said.

Although the river has crested throughout southern Manitoba, the floodwaters were expected to stay high for up to two weeks, straining flood defenses, many of them temporary dikes built from sandbags. Waves would only add to the pressure.
"The waves make the water pound against the dikes so we are watching very carefully," said Debbie MacKenzie, a spokeswoman for the provincial emergency management program.
Emergency crews aided by almost 9,000 Canadian soldiers were checking dikes every 20 minutes and frantic efforts continued to fortify the flood barriers in vulnerable areas.
Extra water pumps were rushed to the town of East Saint Paul outside Winnipeg on Monday after a sandbag dike failed.
In Winnipeg, the 80-year-old Provencher bridge, one of the main arteries across the Red River, was closed to traffic on Monday because engineers feared it had become unstable.
